Stiff Person Syndrome: A Case Report
Advanced Practice Nursing Jennifer C. Ewing, RN, MSN, NP-C, AOCNP®—Associate Editor
Patricia A. Kelly, DNP , APRN, CNS, AOCN®, and Carolyn Kuberski, BSN, RN, OCN®
The case report features a patient who had a diagnosis of a common ty pe of breast 
cancer with an uncommon neurologic syndrome. She had extreme pain and pro -
gressive stiffness with cognitive and functional decline. This article i ncludes the 
pathogenesis and treatment options for a rare, but treatable, autoimmune disor der 
of malignancy called stiff person syndrome. 
Patricia A. Kelly, DNP , APRN, CNS, AOCN®, is a nurse translationist of evidence-based practice and research 
and a genomics consultant and Carolyn Kuberski, BSN, RN, OCN®, is a nursing supervisor of inpatient and 
outpatient oncology, both at the Texas Health Presbyterian Hospital Dallas. The authors take full responsibil-
ity for the content of the article. The authors did not receive honoraria for this work. No ﬁnancial relation-
ships relevant to the content of this article have been disclosed by the authors or editorial staff. Kelly can 
be reached at patriciakelly@texashealth.org, with copy to editor at CJONEditor@ons.org.
Key words: paraneoplastic syndrome; neurological; auto-immune; malignancy; stiff person

A 
64-year-old woman, A.L., was ad -
mitted to the oncology unit for 
neoadjuvant chemotherapy for a 
new diagnosis of breast cancer. On admis-
sion, the patient was alert and oriented. 
She was mildly obese and ambulated with 
a walker. She reported normal bowel and 
bladder function and described a “pain 
and stiffness” in her left leg. 
Her past medical history included fre -
quent falls at home, which she attributed 
to joint disease. Magnetic resonance im -
aging showed spinal stenosis and lumbar 
spine disease. Two months prior to the 
current hospitalization, A.L. had a breast 
biopsy for a right breast mass. Histopathol-
ogy revealed invasive ductal carcinoma 
and ductal carcinoma in situ. Estrogen 
and progesterone receptors were positive, 
HER2-neu receptors were negative, and 
2 of 10 axillary lymph nodes were posi -
tive, which conﬁrmed stage III disease. 
Neoadjuvant treatment was ordered with 
four cycles of doxorubicin, cyclophos -
phamide, and docetaxel every 21 days. 
Because of limited mobility, A.L. received 
her treatments as an inpatient on the on-
cology unit.
After two cycles, A.L. reported in -
creased pain and stiffness in her legs and 
back and spent most of her time in bed. 
She had lumbar spinal decompression 
surgery with little improvement in her 
symptoms. On her third cycle, she report-
ed spasms in her knees when she ﬂexed 
her ankles or inverted her toes. The 
spasms increased when she was anxious 
and with certain noises (e.g., IV pump 
beeping, doors opening and closing). 
She received opioid analgesics for pain 
and baclofen for leg spasms. Differential 
diagnoses included hyper-excitability 
neuromuscular disorders and dystonia, in 
addition to spinal degenerative arthritis. 
After completing chemotherapy, A.L. 
went to a rehabilitation facility and was 
then readmitted to the hospital for a right 
breast mastectomy. After a brief stay on 
the postsurgical unit, she transferred 
to the oncology unit. Her neurologic 
state progressively declined, and she

continually screamed in pain. Her leg 
spasms increased 10-fold with sudden 
noises even at low-volume intensities, 
and she developed contractures in both 
legs (see Figure 1). She was unable to 
focus or hold a short conversation. She 
had to be prompted to swallow food and 
medications, and she lost 30 pounds. 
Serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) 
anti-amphiphysin antibody testing was 
ordered; the results were positive. She 
was diagnosed with paraneoplastic stiff 
person syndrome (SPS).
Stiff Person Syndrome 
SPS is a rare paraneoplastic neurologic 
disorder characterized by underlying 
primary malignancy and progressive im -
pairment of the central nervous system 
(CNS) (Greenlee, 2010). Paraneoplastic 
disorders are immune-mediated and are 
not related to metastatic disease, cancer 
treatment, or disease-related comorbidi -
ties such as infections or coagulopathies 
(Dalmau & Rosenfeld, 2013; Kannoth, 
2012). The syndrome is an antibody 
response to antigens on the surface of a 
cancerous tumor and is thought to be the 
body’s immune response to eliminating 
tumor cells (Byrne, Isakoff, Rincon, &

Contractures

Gudewicz, 2012; Kannoth, 2012). Be -
cause similarities exist between the CNS 
antigens and the tumor antigens, anti -
bodies called onconeural antibodies also 
attack the CNS. The antigen/antibody re -
sponse causes CNS injury and neurologic 
symptoms (Byrne et al., 2012; Graus et al., 
2004; Kannoth, 2012). 
SPS is one of a group of paraneoplastic 
neurologic disorders with diverse on -
coneural antibodies, antigenic targets, 
symptoms, and associated neoplasms 
(Greenlee, 2010). SPS also can be a non-
paraneoplastic disorder and is seen in 
patients with autoimmune diseases such 
as diabetes or thyroiditis (Byrne et al., 
2012; National Institute of Neurological 
Disorders and Stroke, 2010). Overall, SPS 
is rare with an estimated incidence of one 
person per million (Ciccotto, Blaya, & 
Kelley, 2013). Paraneoplastic SPS accounts 
for about 5% of all SPS diagnoses (Rako -
cevic & Floeter, 2012); however, the true 
incidence and prevalence of both non-
paraneoplastic SPS and paraneoplastic SPS 
are unknown (Hadavi, Noyce, Leslie, & 
Giovannoni, 2011; National Organization 
of Rare Disorders, 2010). For the current 
article, SPS is addressed as a paraneoplas-
tic neurologic syndrome. 
Diagnostic criteria for a paraneoplastic 
neurologic syndrome are a cancer diag -
nosis and the presence of onconeural 
antibodies (Graus et al., 2004). SPS is most 
commonly seen with breast and lung can-
cers; however, two-thirds of patients with 
SPS present with occult tumors (Byrne et 
al., 2012; Dalmau & Rosenfeld, 2013). Anti-
amphiphysin antibodies are SPS-speciﬁc 
and are the diagnostic discriminator for 
this paraneoplastic neurologic syndrome 
(Byrne et al., 2012; Graus et al., 2004). 
The anti-amphiphysin antibody blocks 
gamma amino butyric acid (GABA), the 
major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the 
CNS (Byrne et al., 2012). Without GABA, 
motor neurons become hyperexcitable, 
resulting in muscle rigidity and spasms. 
The continuous contractions and lack of 
reciprocal inhibition of both the agonist 
and antagonist muscles cause SPS symp -
toms (Dalakas, 2009).
Clinical Presentation
The presentation of SPS may evolve over 
a few weeks to months (Byrne et al., 2012). 
The clinical criteria for all SPS syndromes 
are: “(1) muscular rigidity in the limbs 
and trunk, (2) continuous co-contraction 
of agonist and antagonist muscles, (3) epi-
sodic spasms precipitated by noise, tactile 
stimuli, or emotional upset, (4) absence 
of any other neurologic disease, and (5) 
positive antibodies for anti-glutamic acid 
decarboxylase (GAD)65 or amphiphysin” 
(Dalakas, 2009, p. 103). 
Patients often have an unsteady gait, a 
wide stance, frequent falls, and abnormal 
eye movements (Byrne et al., 2012; Dal -
akas, 2009; Hadavi et al., 2011). Stiffness, 
rigidity, and spasms of the muscles of 
the head, trunk, and limbs may lead to a 
stiffened, hunched-over posture and dif -
ﬁculty walking. Symptoms are progres -
sive, debilitating, and can lead to limb 
deformities, fractures, inability to walk, 
and being totally bedridden (Dalakas, 
2009). Because the clinical presentation 
mimics other neurologic diseases, SPS is 
misdiagnosed frequently as an anxiety 
disorder, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s 
disease, and somatic disorders (Dalakas, 
2009). 
Diagnostic Testing  
and Treatment
Diagnostic testing includes electro -
physiologic studies that show motor

units continuously ﬁring while at rest 
(Dalakas, 2009). Other diagnostic stud -
ies include CNS imaging and CSF ex -
amination for inflammatory markers. 
Anti-amphiphysin antibody immuno -
histochemistry studies are speciﬁc for 
paraneoplastic SPS (Byrne et al., 2012; 
Dalmau & Rosenfeld, 2013). Antibody 
testing is done on blood and sometimes 
CSF; results may take several weeks 
(Byrne et al., 2012). A clinical cue for 
SPS is improvement after treatment with 
diazepam, a GABA enhancing agent 
(Dalakas, 2009). The treatment for SPS 
has three major approaches (see Table 
1). The treatment goal is stabilization or 
reversal of the CNS damage from onco -
neural antibodies. Treatment responses 
are variable and may be incomplete (Dal-
mau & Rosenfeld, 2013). 
Case Report
A.L. received ﬁve immunoglobulin in -
fusions followed by a ﬁve-day trial of IV 
steroids. She had ﬁve plasma exchanges 
without any improvement in symptoms. 
A.L. then started four weekly infusions 
of rituximab. Two weeks after beginning 
rituximab, A.L. showed marked improve-
ment in her mental status and her ability

Treatment Explanation and Examples
Identiﬁcation and treatment of 
underlying cancer to remove the 
offending antigens 
Careful evaluation, family history assessment, laboratory and 
imaging studies are indicated to identify the tumor origin. 
Treatment is neoplasm speciﬁc. 
Pharmacologic symptom control 
with GABA-enhancing drugs
Examples of GABA-enhancing drugs include:
Sedative anxiolytics
 Diazepam
 Clonazepam
 Lorazepam
 Alprazolam
Antiepileptic drugs
 Gabapentin
 Vigabatrin
 Valproate
Antispasticity drugs
 Baclofen
 Tizanidine
 Botulinum toxin A
Immunotherapy to remove or 
modulate the immune response
IV immunoglobulin (mechanism affecting immunity not totally 
understood)
Rituximab, a B cell-depleting monoclonal antibody
Plasmapheresis (to remove the antibodies)
Corticosteroids (suppress the antibody response)
GABA—gamma amino butyric acid

to focus. She had no recall of the events of 
the past six weeks. Her pain and spasms 
were controlled, and she could ﬂex her 
right foot slightly. A.L. still could not 
walk. She received botulinum toxin injec-
tions in her legs with no improvement in 
symptoms. She subsequently had surgery 
for bilateral release of the Achilles tendon 
and was transferred to a rehabilitation fa-
cility. With casts and leg braces in place, 
A.L. learned to walk again. After one year 
of continuous inpatient care at either 
a hospital or rehabilitation facility, she 
moved back home and continues physi -
cal and occupational therapy. Although 
she has many functional limitations, she 
is able to participate in activities of daily 
living. A.L. remains in remission from her 
breast cancer diagnosis.
Lessons Learned
A.L. had comorbidities that made the 
SPS diagnosis difﬁcult and complicated 
her rehabilitation. When her SPS symp -
toms were at their worst, the healthcare 
team members felt helpless, and some 
perceived A.L.’s behavior to be aggres -
sive and rude. Providing care for her was 
time consuming, and nothing seemed to 
relieve her symptoms. Some team mem -
bers thought A.L. was drug-seeking and 
had psychological issues. Because of her 
progressive symptoms, others thought 
she had undiagnosed metastatic disease. 
Having a diagnosis and understanding 
SPS pathogenesis helped the healthcare 
team establish a treatment plan. In addi -
tion, all team members gained personal 
insight about being judgmental when no 
explanation for pain and other symptoms 
seems to exist.
Feeling like you are the only one with 
a disorder is a lonely prospect for patients 
and family members. The healthcare team 
found SPS resources and support services 
at the National Institute of Neurological 
Disorders and Stroke (
www.ninds.nih  
.gov) and National Organization for Rare 
Disorders (www.rarediseases.org), which 
include assistance programs, clinical trial 
information, as well as physician databas-
es, and genetic counseling information. 
Limited information about SPS is avail -
able in the nursing literature. The authors 
only found two dated articles that focused 
on SPS and diabetes (Spada & Spada, 1994) 
and SPS case management (Laflamme, 
1995). No articles were found regarding 
SPS paraneoplastic syndromes. Therefore, 
paraneoplastic SPS is a fertile topic for 
future research and publications.
SPS is a rare and clinically elusive 
paraneoplastic neurologic syndrome. Un-
derstanding SPS is critical in helping pa -
tients with symptom management, pain 
and mobility issues, as well as achieving 
optimal outcomes.
The authors gratefully acknowledge 
the patient and her family for sharing 
their story, Samir Shah, MD, and Elizabeth 
Winslow, PhD, RN, FAAN, for manuscript 
review, and the librarians at Texas Health 
Presbyterian Hospital Dallas for literature 
searching.
